S141/3.about: Titled ’La campanella’ (’The Little Bell’), one of Liszt’s most famous showpieces, transcribing and elaborating the bell-like finale theme of Paganini’s Violin Concerto No. 2 into a dazzling study in wide, rapid leaps meant to imitate the sound of a ringing handbell.
S141/3.ctx: Originally composed in 1838 as part of an earlier, even more punishing set of Paganini studies, then substantially simplified and revised in 1851 into the version almost always performed today, reflecting Liszt’s lifelong fascination with Paganini’s own violin virtuosity, which he set out to match at the keyboard.
facts: Based on a theme from Paganini’s Violin Concerto No. 2.
Liszt revised and simplified the piece considerably in 1851.
One of the most frequently performed of all Liszt’s études.

S144/3.about: Titled ’Un sospiro’ (’A Sigh’), a lyrical, arpeggio-drenched study built on crossing hands that weave a singing melody between the two, one of Liszt’s most tender and popular pieces despite its considerable technical demands.
S144/3.ctx: Composed in the mid-to-late 1840s as the third of the Three Concert Études, published in 1849, part of Liszt’s effort, across many études of this period, to fuse technical study with genuine lyrical expressiveness rather than pure display.
facts: Its title means ’A Sigh’.
Requires the hands to cross repeatedly to weave a continuous melodic line.
One of the most popular of Liszt’s concert études.

S139/4.about: Titled ’Mazeppa’ after the Ukrainian folk hero, depicting his legendary punishment of being tied to a wild horse and sent galloping across the steppe, before rising, in the poem’s ending, to become a Cossack leader; the étude’s relentless, driving figuration vividly evokes the wild ride, ending in a triumphant march.
S139/4.ctx: Composed in an early version in 1826 and twice revised, reaching its final form in 1851 as the fourth of the Transcendental Études, a cycle of twelve studies Liszt dedicated to his former teacher Carl Czerny; Liszt later also orchestrated the piece as a symphonic poem.
facts: Depicts the legendary Ukrainian folk hero Mazeppa’s wild ride tied to a horse.
Liszt later orchestrated it as a separate symphonic poem.
Part of the Transcendental Études dedicated to Liszt’s teacher, Carl Czerny.

S541/3.about: Liszt’s single most famous piano piece, a piano transcription of his own earlier song setting a poem by Ferdinand Freiligrath urging lovers to love while they still can, since death will come soon enough. Its sweeping, richly ornamented melody has made it, alongside ’La campanella’, one of the pieces most closely associated with Liszt in popular imagination.
S541/3.ctx: Originally composed as a song in 1850 and transcribed for solo piano the same year as the third of the Liebesträume (’Dreams of Love’), a set of three ’notturnos’ each based on a Liszt song.
facts: A piano transcription of Liszt’s own song of the same year.
The third and by far the most famous of the three Liebesträume.
One of the most widely recognized pieces of Romantic piano music.

S244/2.about: By far the most famous of Liszt’s nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies, built on the alternating slow-fast structure of the Hungarian csárdás dance, moving from a brooding, improvisatory opening to an increasingly wild, virtuosic close. Its cadenza has become a fixture of popular culture through its use in numerous cartoons, most famously Tom and Jerry.
S244/2.ctx: Composed in 1847 and based on melodies Liszt believed to be authentic Hungarian folk music, though many were in fact popular urban ’gypsy’ tunes composed by other musicians of the period rather than genuine folk material — a conflation that later scholarship has worked to untangle.
facts: By far the most popular of Liszt’s nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies.
Its melodies, once believed to be authentic folk tunes, are now known to derive largely from popular urban ’gypsy’ music of the period.
Famously used in classic cartoons, including Tom and Jerry.

S178.about: Liszt’s only piano sonata and one of the great structural achievements of Romantic music, cast as a single continuous movement lasting around half an hour, unified by a handful of short themes that are continuously transformed in character across the work rather than developed in the usual sonata manner. Its premiere baffled and divided contemporary critics, including Clara Schumann and Brahms, though it is now regarded as one of the towering works of the piano literature.
S178.ctx: Composed in 1852–53 and dedicated to Robert Schumann (in return for Schumann’s earlier dedication of his own C major Fantasy to Liszt), the sonata represents the fullest expression of Liszt’s technique of ’thematic transformation’, in which a small number of motifs are reshaped, across a large single span, into music of wildly different character.
facts: Cast as a single continuous movement lasting roughly half an hour.
Dedicated to Robert Schumann.
Initially divided critical opinion sharply, including that of Clara Schumann and Brahms.

S514.about: The first and by far most popular of Liszt’s four Mephisto Waltzes, depicting, after a scene from a play based on Goethe’s Faust, the devil Mephistopheles seizing a fiddle at a village wedding and playing a wild dance that seduces Faust and a village girl into the night. A whirling, demonic showpiece of enormous energy and technical difficulty.
S514.ctx: Composed 1859–62, inspired by an episode from Nikolaus Lenau’s version of the Faust legend, and originally conceived as an orchestral work before Liszt arranged it, as he did with many of his pieces, for solo piano, in which form it has become far better known.
facts: Depicts the devil Mephistopheles playing a seductive dance at a wedding, from an episode of the Faust legend.
Originally conceived as an orchestral work before being arranged for solo piano.
The most popular of Liszt’s four Mephisto Waltzes.

S173/7.about: Titled ’Funeral Rites’, a somber, processional piece written in memory of friends who died in the failed Hungarian revolution of 1848–49 against Austrian rule, building from a tolling, bell-like opening to a central section evoking a military charge before subsiding into grief once more.
S173/7.ctx: Composed in 1849 in response to the deaths of several Hungarian patriots, including the composer’s friend, executed after the collapse of the Hungarian uprising against the Habsburg Empire, part of the larger set of ten pieces titled Harmonies poétiques et religieuses.
facts: Written in memory of friends who died in the failed 1848–49 Hungarian revolution.
Part of the larger cycle Harmonies poétiques et religieuses.
Its central section is often heard as evoking a cavalry charge.

S161/7.about: Subtitled ’Fantasia quasi Sonata’ and popularly known as the ’Dante Sonata’, a large-scale, single-movement work depicting, in Liszt’s own words, impressions of Dante’s Inferno, moving between passages of hellish violence and moments of tortured lyricism, closing the second volume of Années de pèlerinage devoted to Italy.
S161/7.ctx: Composed in stages between 1839 and 1849 and revised repeatedly before its 1858 publication, inspired by Liszt’s reading of Dante’s Divine Comedy and by Victor Hugo’s poem on the same subject, the piece anticipates, in its bold formal freedom, the single-movement Piano Sonata Liszt would complete a few years later.
facts: Popularly known as the ’Dante Sonata’.
Closes the second volume of Années de pèlerinage, devoted to Italy.
Revised repeatedly over nearly two decades before its final publication.

S160/6.about: Titled ’Obermann Valley’, the longest and most searching piece of the first volume of Années de pèlerinage, inspired by a novel by Étienne Pivert de Senancour depicting a melancholic wanderer questioning the meaning of existence amid Alpine landscapes.
S160/6.ctx: Composed originally in the mid-1830s during Liszt’s years of travel through Switzerland with the Countess Marie d’Agoult, and substantially revised before publication, the piece reflects the literary, philosophically searching character Liszt brought to much of his early travel-inspired piano music.
facts: Inspired by a novel by Étienne Pivert de Senancour.
The longest piece in the first volume of Années de pèlerinage.
Composed during Liszt’s years of travel through Switzerland with Marie d’Agoult.

S124.about: The first of Liszt’s two piano concertos, cast in a single continuous span of four linked sections rather than the traditional separate movements, unified by a handful of themes transformed throughout — including a famous passage for triangle in the scherzo that drew mockery from some critics as the ’Triangle Concerto’.
S124.ctx: Sketched as early as 1830 and reworked repeatedly over nearly two decades, the concerto was premiered in 1855 with Liszt himself at the piano and Berlioz conducting, part of Liszt’s efforts, as director of music at Weimar, to champion the innovative orchestral and formal ideas of the ’New German School’.
facts: Sketched as early as 1830 but not completed for nearly two decades.
Premiered with Liszt at the piano and Berlioz conducting.
Nicknamed the ’Triangle Concerto’ by unimpressed critics for a prominent triangle passage.

S126.about: A set of variations for piano and orchestra on the medieval ’Dies irae’ chant, dark and percussive, reflecting Liszt’s fascination — shared with Berlioz, whose Symphonie fantastique also uses the same chant — with themes of death and the macabre, reportedly inspired partly by a fresco of the Dance of Death Liszt had seen in Pisa.
S126.ctx: Composed in stages between 1838 and 1849 and revised twice more before its eventual 1865 publication, the piece shows Liszt’s lifelong interest in dark, theatrical subject matter and in the transformation of a single, stark theme across an extended structure.
facts: Based on the medieval ’Dies irae’ chant, also used by Berlioz and later Rachmaninoff.
Reportedly inspired partly by a fresco of the Dance of Death Liszt saw in Pisa.
Took over two decades to reach its final published form.

S97.about: The third and most popular of Liszt’s thirteen symphonic poems, a genre he essentially invented, illustrating, in Liszt’s own preface, the idea that human life is a series of preludes to an unknown song whose first solemn note is sounded by death. Its sweeping, cyclical themes recur throughout, unified by Liszt’s characteristic technique of thematic transformation.
S97.ctx: Composed in 1848 and revised in 1854, loosely inspired by a poem of Alphonse de Lamartine, though Liszt’s own explanatory preface, written after the music, somewhat obscures the work’s actual origins in earlier, differently themed sketches.
facts: Liszt essentially invented the genre of the symphonic poem.
The most popular of his thirteen works in the genre.
Its themes are unified through Liszt’s technique of thematic transformation.

S145/2.about: Titled ’Dance of the Gnomes’, a light, mischievous scherzo built on rapid, glittering figuration suggesting small, scurrying creatures, contrasting the weightier, more overtly virtuosic character of many of Liszt’s other concert études.
S145/2.ctx: Composed in 1862–63, during the period when Liszt was increasingly dividing his time between Rome and his earlier centres of activity, part of a pair of concert études alongside the more lyrical ’Waldesrauschen’.
facts: Its title means ’Dance of the Gnomes’.
Paired with the more lyrical étude ’Waldesrauschen’ in publication.
Prized for its light, glittering touch rather than raw power.
